questions.explanation: Acceptance is judged against the agreed scope as it stands after approved changes, and a new requirement, however reasonable, is a separate request with its own assessment. Letting new scope become a condition of acceptance merges two decisions, so the original work cannot close and the new work escapes impact assessment. Separating them protects both: the delivered product is accepted on what was agreed, and the new need gets a proper decision rather than a concession under deadline pressure.
questions.mindset: Accept what was agreed, and treat what is new as new.

questions.stem: Your agile team builds a public-sector benefits portal and can deploy small, fully tested changes several times a day. IT operations requires every production change to be approved at its weekly change advisory board, which it owns. Finished work now waits up to six days, and the team has started batching changes into large weekly releases, which caused two incidents last month. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Propose to the head of IT operations that low-risk, automatically tested deployments be treated as pre-approved standard changes.
options.rationale: Operations owns the board, so the route to faster approval runs through its owner. Pre-approving a defined class of routine, reversible changes keeps control where it belongs while removing the wait for work that does not need a meeting.

options.text: Raise the more urgent deployments as emergency changes, which the operations process allows to be approved without waiting for the weekly board.
options.rationale: The candidate uses an emergency route for routine work. It erodes trust in the emergency process and, once noticed, usually leads operations to tighten control rather than relax it.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to exempt the team from the change advisory board, given that the team's own delivery process already controls change well.
options.rationale: An exemption bypasses the people accountable for live service, and the team's process controls what is built, not how it lands in production. The candidate goes around the owner of the risk instead of working with them.

options.text: Offer the change advisory board automatic records of every deployment, with test results and rollback steps, so it keeps full oversight.
options.rationale: Pre-approval is only acceptable to operations if it can still see what is happening. Automatic evidence gives the board oversight without a meeting, which is what makes a standard-change category safe to grant.

options.text: Keep the weekly releases but add a fuller regression run before each one, to cut down the incidents that the larger batches are causing.
options.rationale: It treats the symptom. The incidents come from batching, and batching comes from the approval wait, so more testing on large releases adds effort without removing the cause.

questions.explanation: Operational change control exists to protect live services and belongs to whoever runs them, so improving it means working with its owner rather than around it. The usual route is to separate changes by risk: routine, well-tested, reversible changes can be pre-approved as a class with evidence captured automatically, while the board's attention goes to changes that genuinely need it. Large infrequent batches are often a symptom of slow approval, and they raise the very risk that approval was meant to reduce.
questions.mindset: Make the safe path the fast path, and agree it with whoever owns the risk.

questions.stem: You prepare recommendations for the change board of a hybrid programme redeveloping a castle visitor attraction: the building works are plan-driven and the ticketing app is built in sprints. Match each assessed request to the recommendation it supports. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A lift in the gatehouse would open the upper galleries to wheelchair users. The impact assessment is complete, and the €95,000 fits within the remaining change allowance.

Audio-guide downloads in the app have strong demand, but the cost rests on a supplier's verbal figure. The written quote arrives a week before the next board, and no sprint before then would include the work.
A themed courtyard café would cost €140,000 and delay opening by four weeks, and the attraction's operator says it has no staff to run one for at least two years.

options.text: Recommend approval
options.rationale: The benefit is clear, the assessment is complete and the cost fits the allowance. Nothing further would improve the decision, so delaying it only delays the benefit.

options.text: Recommend deferral to the next meeting, pending the written quote
options.rationale: One specific fact is missing and will arrive before waiting costs anything, because no sprint would start the work sooner. Deferring lets the board decide on a real price rather than a verbal one.

options.text: Recommend rejection, recording the reasons for any future request
options.rationale: The benefit cannot be realised, because the operator will not staff the café, so no price makes it good value. Recording why lets a future request show what has changed.

options.text: Recommend approval now, with a ceiling on the supplier's figure
options.rationale: Not used. A conditional approval is tempting for the audio guide, but it commits the board to an estimate it has not seen when waiting a week costs nothing. It earns its place only when delay is expensive.

questions.explanation: A change recommendation follows from what the assessment shows: approve when the case and the impact are both known and acceptable, defer when a specific missing fact will arrive before waiting costs anything, and reject when the benefit cannot be realised at any price. Conditional approvals have their place when delay is expensive, but they commit the project to a figure the board has not seen. Recording the reasons for a rejection is what lets a future request show what has changed.
questions.mindset: Recommend on what the assessment shows, and say exactly what would change the answer.

questions.stem: Your Scrum team builds the companion app for an insulin pump, which is regulated as medical-device software. An auditor has asked to see, for any change, who requested it, who approved it and what testing proved it. The team holds all of this somewhere in conversations and its backlog tool, but not in one traceable form. A team member proposes adding a paper change-request form for every backlog item. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Work with the team and the quality lead to link each backlog item to its request, approval and test evidence inside the backlog tool they already use.
options.rationale: The requirement is traceability, not paperwork. Building the links into the tool the work already runs on gives the auditor a trail that stays accurate because it is the same record the team uses every day.

options.text: Adopt the paper form for every backlog item, because a regulated product needs a change record that an auditor will readily recognise.
options.rationale: The candidate meets the audit with a second record that runs alongside the real one. Within weeks the forms and the backlog drift apart, and the auditor then finds two sources that disagree.

options.text: Show the auditor the backlog tool's history and explain that agile teams record their decisions through conversation rather than forms.
options.rationale: Conversation is how agile teams decide, not how they evidence decisions. The candidate defends the method instead of meeting a legitimate need for a traceable trail in a safety-critical product.

options.text: Introduce the paper form only for items the product owner judges to be safety-related, and keep using the backlog alone for everything else.
options.rationale: A risk-based split sounds proportionate, but it rests on one person's judgement of what is safety-related and still leaves two systems to keep in step. In regulated device software, every change needs a traceable trail.

questions.explanation: Regulated adaptive teams need traceability, not paperwork: the requirement is that each change can be followed from request through approval to verification. Building that evidence into the tools the team already works in produces a record that stays accurate because it is the same record the work runs on, whereas a parallel form drifts out of step with the backlog. The test of any approach is whether an auditor can pick any change and follow its trail without asking anyone to remember.
questions.mindset: Make the trail of every change visible in the place where the work actually happens.

questions.stem: You are fourteen months into building a fire station for a fire and rescue service. No scope has changed, but poor groundworks productivity has left the project with a cost performance index of 0.86 and a schedule performance index of 0.81. The sponsor says the baseline is now meaningless because every report shows red, and asks you to re-baseline to the current forecast so the steering group can track something achievable. What should you do?

options.text: Submit a re-baseline to the change board with the variance history archived, so the steering group tracks progress against an achievable plan.
options.rationale: Going through the board makes it procedurally sound, which is why it is tempting. But with no change to scope or objectives, the re-baseline exists to absorb poor performance, and archiving the history still removes the live measure of it.

options.text: Keep the baseline, and add the forecast completion date and cost to each report so the steering group can track both side by side.
options.rationale: The sponsor's need for an achievable view is legitimate, and a forecast meets it without erasing the variance. The steering group then sees both where the project is heading and how far it has drifted from what was approved.

options.text: Re-baseline only the remaining groundworks packages, where productivity has been worst, and keep the rest of the baseline exactly as it is.
options.rationale: A partial re-baseline hides the variance exactly where it is largest. The candidate narrows the premise rather than questioning it, and the steering group loses sight of the packages that most need attention.

options.text: Keep the baseline and the reports as they are, and explain to the sponsor that variances can only be removed by approved changes.
options.rationale: The rule is right but the response ignores the sponsor's real problem: a report that shows only red tells the steering group nothing about where the project will land. Defending the baseline without adding a forecast leaves that need unmet.

questions.explanation: A baseline is the yardstick for performance, so re-baselining is reserved for approved changes to what the project must deliver, such as scope, objectives or constraints, not for performance that has fallen short. When variances are large, the useful response is to forecast alongside the baseline, so decision-makers see both how far the work is from plan and where it is heading. Replacing the baseline with the forecast erases the signal that tells the organisation its estimates or delivery need attention.
questions.mindset: Report the forecast beside the baseline rather than replacing the yardstick that shows the gap.
